newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss rule out apology for guard in Holocaust case.
newsitem.headline: Swiss rule out apology for guard in Holocaust case.

text.p: The Swiss president on Thursday rejected demands that he apologise to a watchman who fled the country fearing for his safety after saving Holocaust-era documents from shredding at Switzerland's biggest bank.

President Arnold Koller dismissed calls by U.S. Senator Alphonse D'Amato, a leading critic of Swiss banks, that Koller and Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) apologise to former security guard Christoph Meili.
"There is no reason to do so," Koller told Blick when asked if the Swiss government would apologise to Meili.
"Under our system of separation of state powers, Meili's case is in the hands of Zurich prosecutors," he added.

Meili, who was fired by a private security firm, is under criminal investigation for possibly breaking bank secrecy laws by saving the documents. Prosecutors are also looking at whether UBS broke a federal decree barring destruction of Holocaust-era records.
UBS declined to comment on D'Amato's demand for an apology.
"We have said from the beginning that the shredding was a regrettable error and not our intention," UBS spokeswoman Gertrud Erismann told Reuters.

The bank said this week the files that Meili rescued and gave to a Jewish group were records of German properties owned by a subsidiary, including three properties that might have been seized by Nazi authorities from Jewish owners.

Meili was granted permanent U.S. residency this week after fleeing Switzerland with his wife and two young children in April, saying he felt threatened after blowing the whistle in January on the document shredding at UBS.

His revelations that old records were sent to the shredders badly damaged efforts by Swiss banks to combat criticism from world Jewish groups that they are withholding assets left by victims of the Holocaust.

Switzerland's three big global banks faced another serious challenge on Thursday when a U.S. federal judge in New York opened another hearing on three class-action suits by Holocaust victims and their heirs.
Judge Edward Korman was not expected to make a ruling the same day on whether to admit or reject the civil suits, which seek $20 billion and access to all bank records on the Holocaust era.
A new opinion poll on Thursday showed that Switzerland's image abroad was suffering from the past two years of controversy over the fate of accounts left by Jews and others killed by Nazis.
The Swiss weekly L'Hebdo said nearly a third of more than 1,000 Americans and 500 French surveyed said their opinion of Switzerland had deteriorated in recent months because of the row.

Last week Swiss banks took an unprecedented step to appease their critics by breaking traditional secrecy to publish the names of more than 1,870 foreigners who opened Swiss accounts before the end of World War Two in 1945.
Critics said the publication of the list after 52 years of silence and only under mounting international pressure was not in itself enough to restore Switzerland's credibility.

Separately, the U.S. ambassador to Switzerland said on Thursday the Swiss government had to do more to win popular support for a planned "solidarity foundation" to help the country deal with its World War Two past.

"The Swiss government must exert itself to explain the idea of the fund. In the U.S. one would say, 'a good idea deserves to be sold well'," ambassador Madeleine Kunin said in an interview in the Swiss daily newspaper Tages-Anzeiger.
Rightwing opposition has emerged against the foundation, calling into question whether the government's proposal can win approval in a national referendum next year.
The foundation, with capital of around seven billion Swiss francs ($4.6 billion), is supposed to help charities at home and abroad as a way to repair Switerland's image.
